ED chest pain assessment tool

ACS risk tiers (conventional troponin), STEMI equivalents, bleeding risk and dosing, time targets, and alternative diagnoses. The tier follows hard criteria; scores are shown alongside.

STEMI mimics: how to tell them apart (tap each for example ECGs)
  • LVH: concave ST elevation V1–V4 opposite the dominant QRS; suspect MI if the elevation exceeds 1/6 of the S wave.
  • LBBB or paced rhythm: discordance is expected. Sgarbossa-Smith: concordant ST elevation ≥1 mm, concordant ST depression ≥1 mm in V1–V3, or ST elevation ≥1 mm with ST/S ratio ≥25%.
  • Early repolarization: young men, concave ST elevation V2–V4 with J-point notching. Use the Smith-Driver 4-variable formula (≥18.2 favors anterior STEMI).
  • Pericarditis: diffuse ST elevation without reciprocal depression (except V1 and aVR); ST elevation II above III.
  • LV aneurysm: persistent ST elevation in the leads of an old MI, with Q waves and no reciprocal depression.
  • Brugada: coved or saddleback ST elevation limited to V1–V3, no reciprocal depression.
  • Takotsubo: ST elevation to deep T inversion after stress; often needs angiography to separate.
  • Hyperkalemia: global changes, peaked T waves first, no reciprocal depression, quick improvement after calcium and insulin-glucose.
  • Osborn wave: J-point dome in hypothermia (also hypercalcemia, brain injury).
  • Artifact: inconsistent ST elevation or sudden sharp deflections; check the 0.5 Hz high-pass filter.
Not ACS? Findings that point elsewhere
  • ECG: RV strain suggests PE; diffuse ST elevation or electrical alternans suggests pericarditis or tamponade.
  • Chest X-ray: pneumothorax with mediastinal shift means tension pneumothorax; wide mediastinum suggests aortic dissection; pneumomediastinum, effusion or pneumothorax suggests esophageal rupture; enlarged cardiac silhouette suggests pericardial effusion.
  • Hypoxemia with a widened A-a gradient suggests PE.
  • Contrast CT: intimal flap (dissection), pulmonary artery clot (PE), esophageal wall edema or periesophageal fluid (rupture).
  • Bedside ultrasound: pericardial fluid or tamponade; absent lung sliding (pneumothorax).
  • Troponin also rises in heart failure, myocarditis, hypertensive crisis and PE.

HEART: History, ECG, Age, Risk factors, Troponin. TIMI: Thrombolysis In Myocardial Infarction UA/NSTEMI score. GRACE: Global Registry of Acute Coronary Events (in-hospital mortality points). ULN: Upper Normal Limit, the top of your lab’s normal range for troponin (99th percentile of the assay). Wells, PERC, YEARS: pulmonary embolism rules. ADD-RS: aortic dissection detection score. CRUSADE: in-hospital bleeding risk score. CrCl: creatinine clearance (Cockcroft-Gault). HAS-BLED: bleeding risk on anticoagulation. CHA₂DS₂-VASc: stroke risk in atrial fibrillation. MACE: major adverse cardiac events. CCTA: coronary CT angiography. MPI: myocardial perfusion imaging. PCI: percutaneous coronary intervention. Figures: lecture decks (after Aslanger 2021, Ricci 2025 and the STEMI-mimics review cited in the deck). Sources: ESC 2023 ACS, AHA/ACC 2021 chest pain guideline, Granger 2003, HEART and TIMI derivation papers.
